messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh had always taken pride in her work as a tattoo artist. She loved the precision and creativity it required, and her clients adored her attention to detail. But that all changed one fateful day when she was accidentally exposed to toxic chemicals at the shop where she worked. The incident left her feeling shaken and vulnerable, like her body had been invaded. As time passed, Linh began to notice that certain smells triggered a wave of anxiety in her. Hospital or antiseptic scents would transport her back to the moment of exposure, making her feel lightheaded and disoriented. She found herself avoiding hospitals, clinics, and even some medical-themed tattoos that clients requested. It wasn't just the smell itself, but what it represented – a loss of control over her own body. At work, Linh started to feel like she was being watched all the time. She would catch glimpses of people staring at her out of the corner of her eye, or sense that someone was lurking nearby. This feeling of constant surveillance made her skin crawl, and she began to wonder if anyone was monitoring her health after the exposure. Her mind would wander to worst-case scenarios – cancer, organ damage, permanent disability. The paranoia spilled over into her personal life as well. Linh's husband, Tuan, noticed that she had become increasingly withdrawn and isolated. She would hesitate to make decisions or take charge of everyday tasks, fearing that someone else might be controlling the outcome. "I just feel like I'm not in control anymore," she confessed to him one day. "Like my body is a ticking time bomb." As the months went by, Linh's behavior became more erratic. She would turn down tattoo commissions if they involved working with certain chemicals or dyes. Her relationships with clients began to suffer, and her reputation as an artist started to slip. Tuan encouraged her to seek help, but Linh was resistant – she didn't want to admit that the exposure had changed her so profoundly. It wasn't until a particularly grueling tattoo session left her in tears that Linh realized she needed support. She couldn't shake off the feeling of being watched or the constant fear of losing autonomy over her body. With Tuan's prodding, Linh finally agreed to see a therapist, hoping to break free from the suffocating grip of anxiety and reclaim control over her life. As she sat in the waiting room, Linh couldn't help but notice the hospital smell wafting through the air. It made her stomach turn, but this time, instead of fleeing, she took a deep breath and steeled herself for what was to come. Maybe, just maybe, this was the first step towards reclaiming her autonomy – and her art.
